entries.meaning: A domestic animal kept as a pet or a working animal, related to the wolf. ---
examples: Our dog barks at every delivery truck.
She walks her dog before work every morning.
Two dogs got loose in the neighborhood last night.

entries.meaning: A small furry animal commonly kept as a household pet. ---
examples: The cat knocked my glass off the counter.
He's allergic to cats.
Our cat sleeps on the warm laundry.

entries.meaning: A large hoofed animal that people ride and use to pull loads. ---
examples: She's been riding horses since she was six.
The horse wouldn't go anywhere near the trailer.
They keep three horses on ten acres.
entries.contrast: Homophone of hoarse (having a rough voice) — same sound, different word.

entries.meaning: A full-grown female of the cattle, kept for milk and beef. ---
examples: The cows were already back in the barn.
A cow can drink thirty gallons of water a day.
He grew up milking cows before school.

entries.meaning: An adult male of the cattle, usually kept for breeding. ---
examples: Don't cut across that field — there's a bull in it.
The bull got out through a broken gate.
They sold two bulls at the auction.

entries.meaning: A farm animal with a broad snout, raised for pork. ---
examples: The pigs got into the feed shed again.
He raises pigs on a small farm upstate.
A pig is a lot smarter than most people think.

entries.meaning: A horned farm animal kept for milk, meat, and wool. ---
examples: The goats ate half the garden.
She milks the goat twice a day.
A neighbor's goats keep the brush down.

entries.meaning: A small long-eared relative of the horse, used to carry loads. ---
examples: A donkey was tied up outside the store.
Donkeys are calmer than people expect.
They use a donkey to pack supplies up the trail.

entries.meaning: The offspring of a donkey and a horse, bred for hauling. ---
examples: The outfitters run mules down into the canyon.
That mule carried sixty pounds all day.
A mule is stronger than it looks.

entries.meaning: A small breed of horse, short even when fully grown. ---
examples: She got a pony for her eighth birthday.
The kids took turns on the pony.
Three ponies were grazing by the fence.
entries.contrast: A pony is a small adult horse, not a baby one — a young horse is a foal.

entries.meaning: An adult female horse. ---
examples: The gray mare is due to foal in April.
He bought the mare at a spring sale.
Both mares came in from the field on their own.

entries.meaning: An adult male horse kept for breeding. ---
examples: The stallion is kept in a separate paddock.
They flew the stallion in from Kentucky.
Stallions need experienced handling.

entries.meaning: An adult male sheep. ---
examples: The ram butted the gate until it opened.
He keeps one ram with about forty ewes.
Two rams were fighting on the hillside.

entries.meaning: An adult female sheep. ---
examples: Each ewe had twin lambs this spring.
The ewes are kept in the lower pasture.
That ewe won't let anyone near her lamb.
entries.contrast: Pronounced exactly like you — the e and the w are silent.

entries.meaning: An adult female pig, especially one kept for breeding. ---
examples: The sow had a litter of eleven.
They moved the sow into a clean pen.
Two sows were rooting around in the mud.
entries.contrast: The animal is SOW, rhyming with now; the verb sow (to plant seed) is SOH, rhyming with go.

entries.meaning: A large desert animal with one or two humps on its back. ---
examples: We rode camels out to the dunes.
A camel can go for days without drinking.
The camel knelt down so we could climb on.

entries.meaning: A South American pack animal with a long neck and thick wool. ---
examples: They keep two llamas to guard the sheep.
A llama will spit at you if you crowd it.
The llamas followed us the whole way up.
entries.contrast: The double l is a single /l/ sound: LAH-muh.

entries.meaning: A small South American animal related to the llama, raised for its soft wool. ---
examples: The farm keeps about thirty alpacas.
An alpaca is smaller and softer than a llama.
She sells yarn from her own alpacas.

entries.meaning: A long-haired ox of the Central Asian mountains. ---
examples: Yaks carried our gear over the pass.
A yak handles thin air far better than a horse.
We passed a herd of yaks outside the village.

entries.meaning: A small pet rodent with pouched cheeks and a very short tail. ---
examples: Her hamster runs on its wheel all night.
We're watching the neighbor's hamster this week.
Hamsters stuff their cheeks until they're round.

entries.meaning: A small tailless pet rodent with a round body and short legs. ---
examples: The classroom keeps two guinea pigs.
A guinea pig squeaks the second it hears the fridge open.
He cleans the guinea pig cage on Sundays.
entries.contrast: Guinea is said GIN-ee, with a silent u.

entries.meaning: A long slender animal of the weasel family, often kept as a pet. ---
examples: His ferret sleeps most of the day.
Ferrets can squeeze through amazingly small gaps.
She lets the ferret out to run around the room.

entries.meaning: A dog bred for hunting by scent or by sight. ---
examples: The hounds picked up the trail right away.
He keeps a couple of hounds for rabbit hunting.
That hound has the saddest face I've ever seen.

entries.meaning: A rabbit, especially a young one — the affectionate everyday word. ---
examples: The kids saw a bunny under the porch.
She drew a bunny on the birthday card.
There were three bunnies in the nest.

entries.meaning: An animal kept at home for company. ---
examples: The building doesn't allow pets.
Their first pet was a rescue cat.
He talks to his pet like it's a coworker.

entries.meaning: Cows and bulls kept together as farm animals. ---
examples: The cattle were moved to higher ground.
He runs about two hundred head of cattle.
Cattle graze that valley all summer.
entries.contrast: Always plural — no a cattle and no cattles; a single animal is a cow, a bull, or a head of cattle.

entries.meaning: Farm animals raised for food, work, or sale. ---
examples: The storm killed livestock across three counties.
Feed prices hit anyone who raises livestock.
They insure the livestock every year.
entries.contrast: No plural form — never livestocks.

entries.meaning: A large heavy wild animal with thick fur and strong claws. ---
examples: A bear went through our cooler overnight.
Bears come down to the river when the salmon run.
Hang your food where the bears can't reach it.
entries.contrast: Homophone of bare (uncovered).

entries.meaning: A large wild cat of Africa; the male grows a heavy mane. ---
examples: We heard a lion somewhere out in the dark.
Lions hunt mostly at night.
The lion barely looked up at us.

entries.meaning: A female lion. ---
examples: The lioness does most of the hunting.
Two lionesses were lying in the shade.
A lioness will take on anything that comes near her cubs.

entries.meaning: A big striped wild cat from Asia. ---
examples: There are more tigers in captivity than in the wild.
The tiger paced along the fence.
A tiger can bring down an animal twice its size.

entries.meaning: A large spotted wild cat of Africa and Asia. ---
examples: A leopard had dragged the kill up into a tree.
Leopards are almost impossible to spot.
The leopard moved without making a sound.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, LEP-urd — not lee-oh-pard.

entries.meaning: A slender spotted cat, the fastest animal on land. ---
examples: A cheetah can hit sixty miles an hour.
We watched a cheetah cross the road ahead of us.
Cheetahs tire out after about half a minute.

entries.meaning: A powerful spotted cat of Central and South America. ---
examples: A jaguar turned up on a trail camera.
Jaguars bite hard enough to crack bone.
The jaguar swam straight across the river.
entries.contrast: Americans say JAG-wahr; the British say JAG-yoo-ur.

entries.meaning: A large tan wild cat of the Americas. ---
examples: A cougar was spotted near the trailhead.
Cougars mostly stay away from people.
He's lived here thirty years and never seen a cougar.
entries.contrast: The same animal as a mountain lion or a puma — all three names are used in the US.

entries.meaning: A short-tailed wild cat with tufted ears and very wide paws. ---
examples: A lynx crossed the snowmobile track.
Lynxes follow the hares north.
The lynx stood still and stared at us.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like links.

entries.meaning: A dog-like African animal that hunts and scavenges in groups. ---
examples: Hyenas kept us awake most of the night.
A hyena dragged the bone off into the grass.
The hyena has a bite that can crush bone.

entries.meaning: A small wild dog of Africa and Asia. ---
examples: Jackals were calling across the valley.
A jackal slipped past the camp before dawn.
The jackal waited for the lions to finish.

entries.meaning: A wild dog of North America, smaller than a wolf. ---
examples: Coyotes were howling behind the house.
Keep the cat in — there are coyotes around.
A coyote trotted right across the road.
entries.contrast: Two American pronunciations: ky-OH-tee, and KY-oht mostly in the West.

entries.meaning: A small wild dog with a pointed face and a bushy tail. ---
examples: A fox got into the chicken coop.
We see foxes in the yard all the time now.
The fox froze, then bolted.

entries.meaning: A long-eared animal like a large rabbit, with longer legs and no burrow. ---
examples: A hare took off across the field.
Hares turn white here in the winter.
The dog chased a hare halfway to the road.
entries.contrast: Homophone of hair; and a hare is bigger and faster than a rabbit, and lives above ground.

entries.meaning: The largest land animal, with a long trunk and thick gray skin. ---
examples: The elephants came down to the water at dusk.
An elephant can hear sounds we can't.
We watched a young elephant stick close to its mother.

entries.meaning: A huge thick-skinned animal with one or two horns on its nose. ---
examples: There were two rhinoceroses at the water hole.
A rhinoceros sees poorly but hears everything.
The rhinoceros turned and walked off.
entries.contrast: Stress the second syllable, and the h after the r is silent.

entries.meaning: An African animal like a horse, covered in black and white stripes. ---
examples: A herd of zebras crossed right in front of us.
No two zebras have the same stripes.
The zebra wouldn't let the truck get any closer.
entries.contrast: Americans say ZEE-bruh; the British say ZEB-ruh.

entries.meaning: A small graceful antelope of Africa and Asia. ---
examples: A herd of gazelles scattered at the sound.
The gazelle bounded away in long jumps.
Gazelles can outrun almost everything but a cheetah.

entries.meaning: A small tree-climbing primate with a long tail. ---
examples: Monkeys were going through the trash cans.
A monkey grabbed the crackers right out of my hand.
Don't feed the monkeys at the temple.
entries.contrast: Monkeys have tails; apes such as gorillas and chimps do not — English keeps the two words apart.

entries.meaning: A large tailless primate such as a gorilla or a chimpanzee. ---
examples: Gorillas and chimps are apes, not monkeys.
The apes have a whole hillside to themselves.
An ape can learn hundreds of signs.
entries.contrast: Russian обезьяна covers both, but in English an ape has no tail and a monkey does.

entries.meaning: The largest ape, a heavy black-haired animal from central Africa. ---
examples: A silverback gorilla came out of the trees.
Gorillas eat mostly leaves and stems.
The gorilla sat down and ignored us completely.
entries.contrast: Sounds just like guerrilla (an irregular fighter) — same pronunciation, different spelling.

entries.meaning: A small African ape, the closest animal relative to humans. ---
examples: Chimpanzees use sticks to fish for termites.
A young chimpanzee was climbing on the ropes.
The chimpanzee recognized herself in the mirror.
entries.contrast: Stress the last syllable: chim-pan-ZEE.

entries.meaning: A large ground-living monkey with a long doglike face. ---
examples: Baboons raided the camp kitchen.
A baboon was sitting on the hood of the truck.
Roll your windows up or the baboons will get in.

entries.meaning: A large red-haired ape from the forests of Borneo and Sumatra. ---
examples: Orangutans spend almost their whole lives in trees.
An orangutan was untying the knot with her fingers.
The orangutan watched us for a long time.

entries.meaning: An Australian animal that hops on strong back legs and carries its young in a pouch. ---
examples: Kangaroos were all over the golf course.
A kangaroo can clear a fence from a standstill.
We hit the brakes for a kangaroo in the road.

entries.meaning: A small gray Australian animal that lives in trees and eats eucalyptus leaves. ---
examples: A koala was asleep in the fork of the tree.
Koalas sleep about twenty hours a day.
We finally spotted a koala on the third try.

entries.meaning: A large black-and-white bear from China that lives on bamboo. ---
examples: The zoo's panda had a cub last spring.
Pandas eat bamboo almost all day long.
There was a line out the door to see the panda.

entries.meaning: A very slow tree-dwelling animal of Central and South America. ---
examples: A sloth was hanging right over the trail.
Sloths come down from the tree about once a week.
The sloth took a full minute to move one arm.
entries.contrast: Two American pronunciations, SLAWTH and SLOHTH; both are standard.

entries.meaning: A small bushy-tailed rodent that lives in trees. ---
examples: Squirrels got into the attic again.
A squirrel was digging up the flower bed.
The dog lives to chase squirrels.
entries.contrast: Americans squeeze it into one syllable, SKWURL; the British say SKWIR-uhl.

entries.meaning: A small striped ground squirrel of North America. ---
examples: A chipmunk darted under the deck.
Chipmunks stuff their cheeks until they're round.
We counted four chipmunks on the wood pile.

entries.meaning: A large rodent with a long bare tail, common in cities. ---
examples: They found rats behind the dumpster.
A rat ran along the subway track.
The building has a rat problem.

entries.meaning: A stocky burrowing rodent of North America. ---
examples: A groundhog dug a hole under the shed.
Groundhogs can flatten a garden in a week.
The groundhog stood up on its back legs.

entries.meaning: A large rodent with a flat tail that dams streams with cut wood. ---
examples: Beavers dammed the creek behind the house.
A beaver had taken down three young trees.
The beaver slapped its tail and went under.

entries.meaning: A playful river or sea animal with thick fur and webbed feet. ---
examples: Otters were floating on their backs in the kelp.
An otter came up holding a crab.
We watched the otters slide down the bank.

entries.meaning: A heavy burrowing animal with a striped face and powerful claws. ---
examples: A badger had dug up half the pasture.
Badgers are a lot stronger than they look.
The dog knew better than to bother the badger.

entries.meaning: A black-and-white animal that sprays a terrible smell when threatened. ---
examples: Our dog got sprayed by a skunk.
You can smell a skunk a block away.
Skunks come out around dusk.

entries.meaning: A gray animal with a black face mask and a ringed tail that raids garbage. ---
examples: Raccoons tipped over the trash cans again.
A raccoon was washing something in the birdbath.
The raccoon got the latch open somehow.

entries.meaning: A gray North American marsupial that plays dead when it is threatened. ---
examples: An opossum was sitting on the fence.
Opossums eat a huge number of ticks.
The opossum froze in the headlights.
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech it is usually shortened to possum, PAH-suhm.

entries.meaning: A rodent covered in sharp quills. ---
examples: The dog came home full of porcupine quills.
A porcupine was up in the apple tree.
Porcupines chew on anything salty.

entries.meaning: A small spiny animal that rolls into a ball when frightened. ---
examples: A hedgehog was curled up under the hedge.
Hedgehogs are common in English gardens.
She keeps a hedgehog as a pet.

entries.meaning: The only mammal that truly flies, active at night. ---
examples: Bats come out from under the bridge at sunset.
A bat got into the house through the chimney.
Bats eat an enormous number of mosquitoes.
entries.contrast: Same word as a baseball bat — only context tells you which.

entries.meaning: A small slim predator with a long body and short legs. ---
examples: A weasel got into the henhouse.
Weasels can fit through a gap the width of a quarter.
The weasel disappeared into the stone wall.

entries.meaning: A huge sea mammal that breathes through a hole on top of its head. ---
examples: We saw two whales off the point.
A gray whale surfaced right next to the boat.
Whales migrate past here every spring.
entries.contrast: Homophone of wail (a long cry).

entries.meaning: A small sea mammal with a beaked snout, known for being intelligent. ---
examples: Dolphins were riding the wake behind us.
A dolphin jumped clear out of the water.
There's a pod of dolphins out past the buoy.

entries.meaning: A sea mammal with flippers that comes ashore to rest and breed. ---
examples: Seals were sunning themselves on the rocks.
A seal followed the boat for half a mile.
The seals bark all night down at the harbor.
entries.contrast: Spelled and said like the seal on a package — only context separates them.

entries.meaning: A big Arctic sea mammal with long tusks and thick whiskers. ---
examples: A walrus hauled itself up onto the ice.
Walruses use their tusks to climb out of the water.
The walrus must have weighed a ton.

entries.meaning: A large black-and-white sea mammal that hunts in family groups. ---
examples: A pod of orcas went past the ferry.
Orcas hunt together the way wolves do.
The orca rolled over on its side.
entries.contrast: Also called a killer whale, though it is really the largest dolphin.

entries.meaning: A warm-blooded animal that has hair and feeds its young on milk. ---
examples: Whales are mammals, not fish.
Bats are the only mammals that really fly.
Every mammal on the list is nocturnal.

entries.meaning: A gnawing animal such as a mouse, a rat, or a squirrel. ---
examples: The house had a rodent problem all winter.
Rodents have to chew constantly to wear their teeth down.
Rats and squirrels are both rodents.

entries.meaning: An animal of the group that includes monkeys, apes, and humans. ---
examples: Primates have hands that can grip.
Humans are primates too.
The center studies how primates solve problems.

entries.meaning: A mammal that carries its young in a pouch. ---
examples: Kangaroos and koalas are marsupials.
Most marsupials live in Australia.
The opossum is North America's only marsupial.

entries.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals. ---
examples: Wolves are the main predator here.
Deer freeze the moment they sense a predator.
The island has almost no predators.

entries.meaning: The animals that a predator hunts and eats. ---
examples: Owls hunt small prey at night.
The cat dropped its prey on the doormat.
A cheetah has to get close to its prey first.
entries.contrast: Homophone of pray (to speak to God), and it has no plural — never preys.

entries.meaning: An animal that lives on meat. ---
examples: Cats are strict carnivores.
The park's big carnivores are bears and wolves.
A carnivore needs far more territory than a deer does.

entries.meaning: An animal that lives on plants. ---
examples: Cows and deer are herbivores.
A herbivore spends most of the day eating.
The valley supports a lot of large herbivores.
entries.contrast: Americans drop the h: UR-buh-vor; the British say HUR-bi-vor.

entries.meaning: A large or wild animal, especially a frightening one. ---
examples: Something big moved in the brush — some kind of beast.
The dog is a gentle beast despite his size.
The old stories are full of beasts in the woods.

entries.meaning: An adult male deer, rabbit, or goat. ---
examples: He counted six bucks from the stand.
A buck stepped out of the treeline.
The bucks lose their antlers every winter.

entries.meaning: An adult female deer, rabbit, or goat. ---
examples: A doe and two fawns crossed the road.
The does stay together most of the year.
That doe comes through the yard every evening.
entries.contrast: Homophone of dough; the plural does is spelled like the verb does but said DOHZ.

entries.meaning: A fully grown male deer with antlers. ---
examples: A stag was standing at the edge of the field.
Stags fight over territory in the fall.
The stag watched us and didn't move.

entries.meaning: A very young dog. ---
examples: The puppy chewed straight through a phone cord.
They're giving away puppies at the shelter.
A puppy sleeps about eighteen hours a day.

entries.meaning: A young dog, seal, wolf, or similar animal. ---
examples: The seal pups stay on the beach for weeks.
She was just a pup when we got her.
Three wolf pups came out of the den.

entries.meaning: A very young cat. ---
examples: The kittens aren't old enough to leave their mother.
A kitten showed up on our porch.
He fostered six kittens last spring.

entries.meaning: A horse in its first year. ---
examples: The foal was standing within an hour.
Two foals were born the same week.
She hand-raised the foal after its mother died.

entries.meaning: A young male horse. ---
examples: The colt wouldn't leave his mother's side.
They sold the colt as a yearling.
Both colts are out in the far pasture.
entries.contrast: The o is the OH of bolt, not the AH of cot.

entries.meaning: A very young pig. ---
examples: The sow had nine piglets.
A piglet squeezed under the fence.
The piglets follow her everywhere.

entries.meaning: The young of a bear, lion, fox, or similar animal. ---
examples: A bear and two cubs came through the campground.
The lion cubs were play-fighting all afternoon.
Never get between a bear and her cub.

entries.meaning: A deer in its first year, usually still spotted. ---
examples: A fawn was curled up in the tall grass.
The doe left her fawn while she fed.
Two fawns followed her across the yard.

entries.meaning: A hole or tunnel that an animal digs to live in. ---
examples: Rabbits had burrows all through the hillside.
The prairie dogs dove into their burrows.
He stepped in a burrow and twisted his ankle.
entries.contrast: Sounds the same as borough, a district of a city.

entries.meaning: The resting place of a wild animal, especially a large predator. ---
examples: The tracks led back toward the lair.
A wolf will move its lair if people come near.
They finally located the animal's lair.
entries.contrast: One syllable, LAIR — not the two syllables of layer.

entries.meaning: A shelter for a dog, or a business that boards dogs. ---
examples: We board the dog at a kennel when we travel.
He built a kennel out back.
The kennel was full over the holidays.

entries.meaning: A building where horses are kept. ---
examples: She mucks out the stable every morning.
The stables are behind the main house.
We keep the horse at a stable down the road.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the adjective stable (steady); the horse building is a separate noun.

entries.meaning: A wooden cage for rabbits or other small pets. ---
examples: The rabbits live in a hutch by the garage.
He built the hutch out of scrap lumber.
Both hutches need new wire.

entries.meaning: An enclosure of bars or wire for keeping an animal in. ---
examples: The hamster cage needs cleaning.
She won't keep a rabbit in a cage that small.
The cages at the shelter were all full.

entries.meaning: The skin of a large animal, especially once it is taken off for leather. ---
examples: They stretched the hide out to dry.
Buffalo hides were shipped east by the ton.
The boots are made from cow hide.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: Same form as the verb hide (to conceal); the noun means an animal's skin.

entries.meaning: The long hair along the neck of a horse or a male lion. ---
examples: She braided the horse's mane.
A male lion grows a darker mane as he ages.
Their manes were full of tangles.
entries.contrast: Homophone of main (chief, principal).

entries.meaning: One of the long stiff hairs that grow near an animal's mouth. ---
examples: The cat's whiskers twitched.
A seal uses its whiskers to find fish.
One whisker had been broken off.
entries.contrast: Nearly always plural for an animal: a cat has whiskers, and a single one is a whisker.

entries.meaning: The part that sticks out at the back end of an animal. ---
examples: The dog's tail knocked everything off the table.
Squirrels use their tails for balance.
He stepped on the cat's tail by accident.
entries.contrast: Homophone of tale (a story).

entries.meaning: The foot of an animal that has claws and soft pads. ---
examples: The dog gave me his paw.
She checked the puppy's paws for cuts.
There were muddy paw prints all over the couch.

entries.meaning: A sharp curved nail on an animal's foot. ---
examples: The cat sank her claws into the arm of the chair.
A bear's claws are as long as your fingers.
He clipped the dog's claws a little too short.

entries.meaning: A long pointed tooth used for gripping or tearing. ---
examples: The wolf bared its fangs.
One fang was chipped.
You could see the dog's fangs when he yawned.

entries.meaning: The long nose and jaws that stick out from an animal's face. ---
examples: The pig pushed its snout under the fence.
A bear's snout is its best tool.
Their snouts were black with mud.

entries.meaning: An animal's nose and mouth, or a strap that fits over them. ---
examples: The dog rested his muzzle on my knee.
The horse's muzzle had gone gray with age.
They put a muzzle on him at the vet.
entries.contrast: Two meanings: the animal's own nose and mouth, and the strap you buckle over them.

entries.meaning: A hard pointed growth on the head of cattle, goats, or sheep. ---
examples: The goat caught its horns in the fence.
A bull's horns curve forward.
One horn had broken off years ago.

entries.meaning: One of the branched bony growths on a deer's head. ---
examples: The buck's antlers had eight points.
He found a shed antler in the woods.
Antlers grow back bigger every year.
entries.contrast: Antlers are branched, grow on deer, and drop off each year; horns are unbranched and permanent.

entries.meaning: A very long tooth that sticks out of an animal's mouth.
examples: The elephant's tusks were nearly six feet long.
A walrus uses its tusks to haul out onto the ice.
One tusk was worn down to a stub.
